more.title: Newly discovered barrier could explain why nucleic acid medicines remain trapped inside cells
more.summary: Researchers from the Department of Chemistry at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) and their collaborators have discovered a barrier that may prevent some promising nucleic acid medicines from reaching their targets inside subcellular compartments. Published in Nature Cell Biology, the findings could help guide the development of more effective drug delivery strategies.

more.title: Denisovan remains and an unknown archaic human lineage discovered in southern China
more.summary: An international team of researchers, including first author Song Xing, a researcher affiliated with the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana (CENIEH), has just published a study in the journal Nature that analyzed four fossil teeth recovered from two caves in southern China.

more.title: Income inequality is rising while becoming more similar across countries
more.summary: Inequality is a much-debated issue in politics and society. International comparative research shows that income inequality has risen in most countries. At the same time, however, the differences in disposable income levels between countries have narrowed.

more.title: Strawberries, cucumbers and lemon basil show promise for future moon and Mars menus
more.summary: As NASA prepares for future missions to the moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

more.title: Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact
more.summary: Arriving at the site of humankind's first planetary defense experiment, the European Space Agency's Hera mission has found a miniature world of surprises. Dimorphos—the small asteroid whose orbit around a second, larger asteroid was deflected by a spacecraft impact—now has one face flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling chaotically.

more.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
more.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

more.author: Dan McCarthy
more.summary: See more from Canary Media’s “Chart of the Week” column . Solar energy is poised to become the No. 2 source of electricity in China, capping off a remarkable ascent over the last decade. Hydropower has historically been the runner-up on China’s grid — a distant second to coal, which provides more than half the…

more.title: New technologies help Natural History Museum uncover 92 species in its transformed gardens
more.summary: The Natural History Museum's transformed gardens in South Kensington are revealing new insights into London's urban wildlife. Among the 92 species recorded at the site for the first time between its reopening in July 2024 and the end of 2025 are the striking emperor moth and small red-eyed damselfly.

more.title: AI simulates electron hops over far longer times than conventional quantum calculations
more.summary: To predict how a material will behave, we need to know which atoms are located where. This allows us, for example, to explain whether a material is suitable as a catalyst for certain chemical reactions. But often, that is not enough: even if all the atoms stay exactly where they are, the distribution of electric charge within the material can change dramatically.

more.title: Rocks under the lens: A simple microscope opens new possibilities for quantitative rock analysis
more.summary: Rocks hold a wealth of information about Earth's history. The size, shape and orientation of the mineral grains that make them up can reveal how rocks formed, deformed and changed deep beneath the surface. However, collecting this information has traditionally required specialized equipment and time-consuming analysis.

more.title: Fiber-optic sensing unearths surprising complexity in small California earthquake
more.summary: More than 20,000 earthquakes are located worldwide each year, but the vast majority of those are small—many too small to be felt by humans. Scientists have historically assumed most of these small earthquakes break as small, circular ruptures in which the rocks in a fault slip past each other in a single, smooth motion, and the crack spreads outward from one point like a ripple in a pond, unlike the behavior of most…

more.title: Using a drone and a poop-sniffing dog, scientists perform health checks on endangered orcas
more.summary: Every fall for the last few years, Deborah Giles starts her workday with one question in mind: Where are the orcas?

more.title: 'That's when the chaos began': The fall of the Berlin Wall in the words of East and West Germans
more.summary: Germany's far right is on the rise, with current polls suggesting the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has the backing of 28% of voters nationally. This makes it the most popular party in the country, ahead of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats at 20%.

more.title: Can storybook characters teach children about perseverance?
more.summary: Many storybooks incorporate messages about not giving up when faced with a challenge—something that perhaps isn't surprising given that perseverance is an important factor for learning and long-term success.

more.title: Why a warmer atmosphere doesn't guarantee more water in rivers
more.summary: Austria experienced an exceptional drought in 2026. From the start of the year until the end of October, rainfall was around a third lower than the long-term average. The consequences are low river flows and groundwater levels. But how is water availability linked to global warming? Shouldn't a warmer atmosphere, which can hold more water vapor, also lead to more rainfall?

more.title: AI could be used to write your child's report. Is this a problem?
more.summary: For many families, it's that time of year when school reports land in parents' inboxes.

more.title: The world is experiencing a string of abnormally hot days—and records are being shattered
more.summary: We're becoming used to seeing records being broken whenever we look at data telling us about Earth's climate. Whether it's the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, heat in the ocean or shrinking sea ice around the poles, the signs of human-caused climate change are all around us.

more.title: Melting Barents Sea ice gives Eastern Europe's farmers a spring boost
more.summary: For decades, sea ice in the Barents Sea, a part of the Arctic Ocean north of Norway and Russia, has been shrinking as the Arctic warms. The loss of so much ice can alter weather patterns well beyond the polar region, including in Europe. But how these changes might affect vegetation growth and agricultural production is less well understood.

more.title: Is AI‑assisted thinking devaluing business degrees?
more.summary: As AI models improve, high-quality knowledge is becoming easier to access. A degree therefore has to certify something more durable than the ability to retrieve knowledge or produce a plausible answer. It must show that a student can exercise judgment, make decisions and defend them.
